dunkeld.intro: Dunkeld and Birnam face each other across the Tay, and their old trees line both banks. On the Birnam side, an oak said to be the last of Shakespeare's Birnam Wood stands a few steps from a broader sycamore that local tourist literature calls an oak. Upstream on the Inver Walk is Niel Gow's Oak, named for the fiddler. Behind the cathedral, the Parent Larch survives from a planting of 1738, beside a topless Douglas fir credited with a British record girth. All of them are free to walk up to.
dunkeld.meta_description: The Birnam Oak of Macbeth, Niel Gow's Oak and the 1738 Parent Larch: Dunkeld's old trees on the Tay, their stories and how to walk to each.
dunkeld.question_meta: Dunkeld's oldest tree is the Birnam Oak, a hollow sessile oak on the Tay put at roughly 500 to 600 years from its size.
dunkeld.question_answer: The Birnam Oak, on the riverside path along the Tay's south bank, is the oldest tree here, put at roughly 500 to 600 years from its size. No record dates it. Niel Gow's Oak and the Birnam Sycamore are each thought to be around 300 years old, and the Parent Larch behind the cathedral was planted in 1738.
dunkeld.question_context: The Birnam Oak carries the town's most famous story. Local tradition makes it the last survivor of Birnam Wood, the forest that comes to Dunsinane in Macbeth, though the real Macbeth died in the 11th century and the tree is far younger. Its age is an estimate from its size, and the sources measure that size differently. The International Oak Society gives a girth of 7 metres and a height of 27, while Wikipedia calls the trunk 5.5 metres wide. The trunk is hollow for its first few metres and its long lower limbs rest on timber props. The ages of the others are just as soft. Niel Gow's Oak is roughly 300 years old, and the Birnam Sycamore, a few steps from the oak, is put at about 300 by a tourism source. The one firm date in Dunkeld belongs to the Parent Larch, sole survivor of larches planted behind the cathedral in 1738, whose seed raised later plantings across the Atholl estates. Beside it, a Douglas fir was planted in 1846, according to a single source. If you know better dates for any of them, tell us.

faq.q: Is the Birnam Oak really part of Macbeth's Birnam Wood?
faq.a: Only by tradition. Macbeth died in the 11th century and the oak is far younger, at roughly 500 to 600 years. It may have stood when Shakespeare is believed, but not documented, to have visited Perthshire in 1589.

faq.q: Can you see Dunkeld's old trees on one walk?
faq.a: Yes. The Birnam Oak and the Birnam Sycamore stand a few steps apart on the riverside path on the south bank of the Tay. Niel Gow's Oak is upstream on the Inver Walk, and the Parent Larch and the Dunkeld Douglas Fir stand together in the grounds behind Dunkeld Cathedral. All are free.

faq.q: Why is the Parent Larch famous?
faq.a: It is the sole survivor of European larches planted here in 1738 for the Duke of Atholl, and its seed raised later plantings across the Atholl estates, which earned it the nickname Mother of Millions. The claim that these were the first larches in Britain is disputed.

faq.q: How do you get to the trees by train?
faq.a: Dunkeld and Birnam railway station serves both villages. The Birnam trees are a few minutes' walk from Birnam village, and the cathedral is in Dunkeld, across the Tay.

wolverhampton.intro: Wolverhampton's oldest trees are yews on its western and southern edges, and all of them were noticed long before anyone measured them. In Tettenhall three stand in a line beside a church that burned in 1950; they were called venerable in 1804. Codsall's churchyard yews were very ancient to a county historian in 1801. On the wooded hill above Himley Hall, a poet praised an ancient yew in 1791, and at Boningale a lone yew may be the one in a watercolour from that same year. None has a reliable age.
wolverhampton.meta_description: The yews of Tettenhall, Codsall, Himley Hall and Boningale, written about since 1791: Wolverhampton's oldest trees and how to reach each.
wolverhampton.question_meta: Nobody has dated Wolverhampton's oldest trees; the Tettenhall yews, venerable in 1804 and nearly seven metres round, are the largest.
wolverhampton.question_answer: Nobody has put a reliable age on any of them, so the honest answer is the best-recorded. The three yews in Tettenhall churchyard are the largest, the biggest measured at 693 centimetres round in 1999, and they were described as venerable in 1804. The yews on the hill above Himley Hall run them close, the largest about 640 centimetres round.
wolverhampton.question_context: Yews are the hardest trees in Britain to date. Their heartwood rots out with age, leaving nothing to count, and girth turns into age only through growth rates that vary from tree to tree. So the evidence here is the written record. In Tettenhall a magazine noted venerable yews in 1804, and in 1899 a visitor declared the great yew more than 2,000 years old, an opinion no modern survey supports. At Codsall a county historian called the churchyard yews very ancient in 1801. Above Himley Hall, a poem of 1791 praised a very ancient yew of extraordinary size on the hill, and a yew there measured 20 feet 10 inches in 1844, close to today's largest at about 21 feet. Whether they are the same tree cannot be proved. At Boningale a watercolour of 1791 shows a yew at the church, read by the Ancient Yew Group as the one standing today. Beyond those records, nobody can put a number on any of them. If you know better, tell us.

faq.q: How big are the Tettenhall yews?
faq.a: The largest, nearest the church, measured 693 centimetres round at a foot off the ground in 1999, and the one furthest from the church 681 centimetres at the base. The middle one is a burnt-out hollow shell.

faq.q: Are any of the yews 2,000 years old?
faq.a: A visitor claimed so for the great Tettenhall yew in 1899, but it was an opinion, not a measurement, and no modern survey supports it. None of these yews has a reliable age.

faq.q: Can I visit the yews for free?
faq.a: Yes. Tettenhall, Codsall and Boningale are open parish churchyards, and Himley Park is free to walk, though Himley Hall itself charges separately.

faq.q: Where are Himley Hall and Boningale?
faq.a: Himley Hall is on the Dudley edge, about 8 kilometres south-west of Wolverhampton city centre. Boningale is a Shropshire village about 10 kilometres west, near Albrighton station.

cannock-chase.intro: At Shugborough, on the edge of Cannock Chase, a yew that the National Trust calls Europe's widest has spread sideways by rooting its own branches, until its main stem is almost impossible to reach. In Brocton Coppice, the part of Staffordshire with the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees, walkers have named two gnarled oaks after film trees, Groot and Treebeard. None of the three has a reliable age, and only Shugborough charges for entry.
cannock-chase.meta_description: Shugborough's sprawling yew, called Europe's widest, and the Groot and Treebeard oaks of Brocton Coppice: Cannock Chase's old trees and how to find them.
cannock-chase.question_meta: None of Cannock Chase's best-known old trees has a reliable age; the Groot oak of Brocton Coppice has been guessed at 500 years or more.
cannock-chase.question_answer: Nobody has dated any of the three properly. The Groot oak in Brocton Coppice has been guessed at 500 years or more, but only in a photographer's caption. The Great Yew of Shugborough was estimated at 250 to 300 years old in 1898, an estimate we have not been able to check.
cannock-chase.question_context: Brocton Coppice is the stronger answer for the Chase as a whole. It holds the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees in Staffordshire, old oak woodland among birch, protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Two of its oaks have names. The Groot Tree, gnarled enough to earn one, was photographed in 2021, described in 2023 and mapped in 2025, and its age rests on a single guess. The Treebeard Oak, up a narrow path about five minutes from the Sher Brook stepping stones, has a hollow belly and no date at all. A newspaper in 2022 said trees in the Coppice go back two or three centuries, some to the time of Henry VIII, but that describes the wood, not either trunk. Shugborough's yew is better measured but no better dated. Its crown was given a circumference of 261 feet in 1898 and about 171 metres by 1992, because its branches root where they touch the ground. A writer in 1898 thought it 250 to 300 years old. If you know a better date for any of them, tell us.

faq.q: Is the Shugborough yew really the widest in Europe?
faq.a: The National Trust describes it as Europe's widest yew, and it carries that reputation. No published contest settles it, but its crown was recorded at about 171 metres round in 1992.

faq.q: Why are the Brocton Coppice oaks called Groot and Treebeard?
faq.a: Walkers say their gnarled trunks look like the walking trees of Guardians of the Galaxy and The Lord of the Rings. The Groot Tree is listed under that name on photo and walking sites, and Staffordshire Live wrote up the Treebeard oak in 2022.

faq.q: How do I find the Treebeard oak?
faq.a: From the Punchbowl car park near Milford, walk down to the Sher Brook stepping stones, turn right up the next main path, then right up a narrow path, bearing right at the split and climbing a steep slope. The oak is on the right, about five minutes from the stones.

faq.q: Do I have to pay to see these trees?
faq.a: The Shugborough yew is inside the National Trust estate, which charges for the park and gardens. Brocton Coppice is open woodland and free.

scone.intro: David Douglas, the plant collector whose name the Douglas fir carries, was born in Scone in 1799 and worked as an under-gardener in the palace grounds. Scone Palace says the giant Douglas fir in its gardens was raised from the first seed he sent home from North America, in 1826, though other references date his introduction of the species to 1827. The palace prizes it for its size. It stands in paid gardens just outside Perth, near a Pinetum of rare conifers gathered by the 4th Earl of Mansfield.
scone.meta_description: The Douglas fir at Scone Palace, raised from David Douglas's first seed sent home from North America: its story and how to visit.
scone.question_meta: Scone's best-known old tree is the Douglas fir at Scone Palace, raised from seed David Douglas sent home in 1826.
scone.question_answer: The Douglas fir in the gardens of Scone Palace is the notable old tree here. The palace says it was raised from the first seed David Douglas sent home from North America, in 1826, which puts it somewhere under two centuries old.
scone.question_context: David Douglas was born in the village of Scone in 1799 and worked as an under-gardener in the palace grounds before moving to Glasgow Botanic Gardens and then the Royal Horticultural Society. The palace's own account is that this fir was raised from the first seed he sent home from North America, and it gives that seed the date 1826. Wikipedia and other references put his introduction of the species to Britain in 1827, so the year depends on which source you read. Either way, the palace says the tree was raised from that seed, which tells you its origin rather than the year it was planted, so its age is a bracket rather than a number. We have not found a published girth or height from a source we could read, though the palace prizes it for its size. It was photographed in May 2025 under the title the Famous Scone Palace Douglas Fir. Other Douglas firs grow in the palace's Pinetum, the collection of rare conifers gathered by the 4th Earl of Mansfield in the 19th century, so ask at the palace if you are unsure which tree is the one. If you know its measurements, tell us.

faq.q: Who was David Douglas?
faq.a: A plant collector born in Scone in 1799, who worked as an under-gardener at Scone Palace before moving to Glasgow Botanic Gardens and the Royal Horticultural Society. The Douglas fir carries his name.

faq.q: How old is the Scone Palace Douglas fir?
faq.a: Under two centuries. The palace says it was raised from seed Douglas sent home in 1826; other references date his introduction of the species to 1827. Nobody has published its planting year.

faq.q: Do I have to pay to see it?
faq.a: Yes. The tree is in the gardens and grounds of Scone Palace, which charge for entry. The palace's website lists opening times and prices.

blair-atholl.intro: In February 2009 a grand fir in Diana's Grove, beside Blair Castle, was measured for the Tree Register at 62.70 metres, then the second tallest tree in the United Kingdom. The same two-acre grove is listed with the UK's tallest Japanese larch and tallest red fir. The 2nd Duke of Atholl laid out the gardens before 1740, but the great storm of 1893 blew down many trees, and most of what stands today was replanted by the 7th Duke. The grove lies in the castle grounds, open in season.
blair-atholl.meta_description: Diana's Grove at Blair Castle, where a grand fir measured 62.70 metres in 2009, then the UK's second tallest tree: its story and how to visit.
blair-atholl.question_meta: Blair Atholl's record tree is the grand fir in Diana's Grove, measured at 62.70 metres in 2009; nobody has dated it.
blair-atholl.question_answer: The grand fir in Diana's Grove is the tree to see, measured at 62.70 metres in 2009, but nobody has dated it. The grove was laid out before 1740 and largely replanted after the storm of 1893, which tells you about the grove rather than this tree.
blair-atholl.question_context: Diana's Grove is a two-acre stand of tall conifers around a statue of Diana in the grounds of Blair Castle. The 2nd Duke of Atholl spent three years laying out the gardens before 1740, and some of the first European larches in the country were planted here, followed by North American firs. The 7th Duke brought in Japanese larch in 1884. In 1893 a great storm blew down many trees and destroyed the statue, and the 7th Duke replaced it and replanted, so most of the trees seen today are his. The grand fir was measured for the Tree Register in February 2009 at 62.70 metres, which made it the UK's second tallest tree at the time; a visitor in 2026 gave 63.5 metres. The ranking has moved on since, but the tree still stands. Tourism pages also list the UK's tallest Japanese larch here at 44 metres and its tallest red fir at 39. Paths radiate from the statue, one aligned with the castle's front door, and two 18th-century bridges cross the Banvie Burn towards the ruined St Bride's Kirk. If you know when the grand fir was planted, tell us.

faq.q: How tall is the grand fir in Diana's Grove?
faq.a: It was measured for the Tree Register at 62.70 metres in February 2009, then the second tallest tree in the UK. A visitor in 2026 gave 63.5 metres.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket for Diana's Grove?
faq.a: The walled Hercules Garden needs a gardens ticket, but whether Diana's Grove itself does is not clear from what Atholl Estates publishes. Check their website before you go; the castle grounds keep a season from April to October.

faq.q: How do I get to Blair Castle by train?
faq.a: Blair Atholl has a station on the Highland Main Line, and Blair Castle is about a kilometre from the village.

meikleour.intro: Guinness World Records lists the Meikleour Beech Hedge as the tallest and longest hedge in the world, about 30 metres high and 530 metres long beside the A93 south of Blairgowrie. It was planted in the autumn of 1745 on the Meikleour estate, and local tradition says the men who planted it left for Culloden and never came back, so it grew up instead of out. It is trimmed roughly once a decade and seen from the public road, free, in any season.
meikleour.meta_description: The Meikleour Beech Hedge, planted in 1745 and listed by Guinness as the world's tallest hedge at about 30 metres: its story and where to see it.
meikleour.question_meta: Meikleour's famous trees are the beeches of its hedge, planted in the autumn of 1745 and now about 30 metres tall.
meikleour.question_answer: The Meikleour Beech Hedge was planted in the autumn of 1745, which makes its beeches around 280 years old. It is a line of trees rather than a single trunk, about 530 metres long beside the A93.
meikleour.question_context: The hedge was planted by Jean Mercer and her husband, Robert Murray Nairne, on the Meikleour estate in the autumn of 1745. Local tradition says the men who planted it left to fight at Culloden and never returned, so nobody cut it and it grew tall, a story the sources tell as tradition rather than record. Guinness World Records lists it as the tallest and longest hedge, about 30 metres high and 530 metres long. In 1906 the tree writers Elwes and Henry described it running 580 yards, with stems planted about 18 inches apart and an average height of 95 feet, figures for a row of trees rather than one trunk. It is still trimmed, roughly every ten years, and the most recent trim, in late 2019, was the first in almost two decades. The newest photographs we have found are from 2018, so if you pass, tell us how it looks. The hedge is the boundary of private estate land and is seen from the public A93, free at any time. In late October and November the beech turns copper.

faq.q: Is the Meikleour hedge really the tallest in the world?
faq.a: Guinness World Records lists it as the tallest and longest hedge, about 30 metres high and 530 metres long.

faq.q: Can you visit the Meikleour Beech Hedge?
faq.a: It is seen from the public A93 between Perth and Blairgowrie, free and at any time. The hedge marks private estate land, so it is a view from the road.

faq.q: How often is the hedge cut?
faq.a: Roughly every ten years. The most recent trim, in late 2019, was the first in almost two decades.

faq.q: When is the hedge at its best?
faq.a: Late October into November, when the beech wall turns copper and russet.

balfron.intro: Balfron's Clachan Oak is known locally as the hanging tree. Iron hoops hold its hollow trunk together, and a local visitor guide says people were once chained to it as punishment for petty crimes. The same guide dates it to at least 1553, and local legend ties it to William Wallace and Rob Roy MacGregor, though one account doubts it is old enough for Wallace. It stands in the old part of the village, the Clachan, about 28 kilometres from Stirling, with no gate or fee reported.
balfron.meta_description: The Clachan Oak in Balfron, the hoop-bound hanging tree said to date to at least 1553: its story, its legends and where to find it.
balfron.question_meta: Balfron's oldest tree is the Clachan Oak, the hoop-bound hanging tree thought to date back to at least 1553.
balfron.question_answer: The Clachan Oak is Balfron's oldest tree, thought by a local visitor guide to date back to at least 1553, which would make it more than 470 years old. Nobody has published a girth or a scientific age to confirm it.
balfron.question_context: The oak stands in the Clachan, the old part of Balfron, and it is known locally as the hanging tree. Iron hoops hold its hollow trunk together, and a local visitor guide says people were once chained to it as punishment for petty crimes. The same guide says it is thought to date back to at least 1553 and possibly further, without saying where the date comes from, so it is the local account rather than a measurement. Legend asks more of it. Local stories tie the oak to William Wallace and to Rob Roy MacGregor, but one account thinks it unlikely the tree is old enough for Wallace, who died in 1305. It was photographed in November 2012, the hoops plain on its trunk, and again in February 2022, and an observation logged at the spot in 2025 suggests it still stands. The species is confirmed only as oak, and no girth or height has been published. If you know whether it is pedunculate or sessile, or where the 1553 date comes from, tell us.

faq.q: Why is the Clachan Oak called the hanging tree?
faq.a: A local visitor guide says people were once chained to it as punishment for petty crimes, and the name has stuck. Iron hoops now hold its hollow trunk together.

faq.q: Is the Clachan Oak connected to William Wallace?
faq.a: Local legend says so, and also links it to Rob Roy MacGregor. One account thinks the tree unlikely to be old enough for Wallace, who died in 1305.

faq.q: Where is the Clachan Oak?
faq.a: In the Clachan, the old part of Balfron village in Stirlingshire, about 28 kilometres from Stirling. No gate or entry fee is reported.
